catalog_quote: テンボ語の声調については特徴的なことが 2 つある。1 つは、声調の調値がバンツー祖語や周辺言語と比べて逆転していることである（梶 1994, Kaji 1996）。もう 1 つは、名詞類の声調のパターンが単語を構成するモーラ数が増えるに従って等比級数的に増えていく無制限タイプであることである（梶 1978, 2001b）。さらに、声調実現の単位が音節ではなくモーラである点、また単独形の声調が基本となるというのもテンボ語の特徴である。[...] テンボ語の基本声調は他の多くのアフリカ諸語同様、高平板調 H (high) と低平板調 L (low) の 2 つである。尤も、音声的には H と L の組み合わせにより (1a) のように下降調 F (falling) と (1b) のように上昇調 R (rising) が生じる。[...] テンボ語には母音の長短の区別はない。かつての母音の長短の区別は失われ 1 モーラ化している。[...] テンボ語の TRU は音節ではなくモーラである。
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tembo (Kitembo) is not in the catalog. The three title-keyword items are all false attachments: Philippson 1991 (thesis on East African Bantu tone/accent, already on file under bemb1257 with a text layer) has zero mentions of Tembo — its Group I sample is nande, konzo, hunde, shi, fuliru (Tableau 1, p. 70), and it links to temb1270 only via Maho's autotranslation of j.d.53 (Shi); it says Group I languages are tonal (Hunde reduces HH to HL, p. 412) and that penultimate demarcative accent replaced tone only in Group III (Nyoro/Tooro). Möhlig 1969 (two duplicate Glottolog records) deals with Dciriku, Hehe, Chaga and Shi, is print-only (ZDMG Suppl. I; no digital copy found on MENAdoc or elsewhere), and is attached to Tembo by a computerized assignment. The substantive Tembo literature is Kaji's first-hand work (1978, 1994, 2001, 2021, all open and already on file), which uniformly describes Tembo as a polymoraic tone language (H/L on each mora; contrasted with accentual Haya and bound-accent Swahili) and never posits word stress; Kaji 1996 JALL remains paywalled. Best statement: Kaji 2001, p. 37 English summary.fr, HAL API, MENAdoc, De Gruyter) only.

new_statements.quote: テンボ語の声調については特徴的なことが 2 つある。1 つは、声調の調値がバンツー祖語や周辺言語と比べて逆転していることである（梶 1994, Kaji 1996）。もう 1 つは、名詞類の声調のパターンが単語を構成するモーラ数が増えるに従って等比級数的に増えていく無制限タイプであることである（梶 1978, 2001b）。さらに、声調実現の単位が音節ではなくモーラである点、また単独形の声調が基本となるというのもテンボ語の特徴である。[...] テンボ語の基本声調は他の多くのアフリカ諸語同様、高平板調 H (high) と低平板調 L (low) の 2 つである。
new_statements.translation: Two things are characteristic of Tembo tone. One is that the tone values are reversed compared with Proto-Bantu and the neighbouring languages (Kaji 1994, 1996). The other is that the tone patterns of nominals are of the unrestricted type, increasing geometrically as the number of moras making up the word increases (Kaji 1978, 2001b). Further characteristics of Tembo are that the unit of tone realization is the mora, not the syllable, and that isolation-form tone is basic. [...] The basic tones of Tembo are, as in many other African languages, two: level high H and level low L.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tembo is described as a pure ('unrestricted', 2^n-pattern) mora-counting tone language with lexical H vs L on every mora (F and R as HL/LH combinations), downdrift but no downstep, and no vowel-length contrast; Kaji (1978, 2001, 2021) explicitly contrasts it with pitch-accent/accentual Bantu languages. None of his opened descriptions mentions word stress, dynamic accent or penultimate prominence for Tembo.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal notes: word-initial syllabic nasal bears its own tone; rising tone is realized as H word-initially; some patterns exceed 2^n, e.g. FH, LFL.)
new_statements.domain_note: Isolation (citation) forms are stated to be tonally basic; description is of word-level lexical tone, mainly Bunyakiri dialect, tone said to be identical across dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: All of Kaji's data are Tembo (Échítembo) of eastern DRC, glottocode temb1270, ISO tbt; the 2021 chapter states examples are mainly from the western Bunyakiri dialect and that tone is identical across the four dialects (Mbugu, Buloho, Bunyakiri, Ufamandu). Kaji notes Maho's JD531 code conflates Tembo with Shi (JD53); Kaji himself uses J.57. Not to be confused with Tembo (Motembo) of Equateur (tmv).

new_statements.quote: With Tembo it is demonstrated that in this language each mora in principle should be marked either as high, low, falling or rising (the last two being combinations of high and low). The number of partterns increases in geometric progression. Tembo, therefore, can be characterized as a polymoraic tone language. In Haya, however, the number of tone patterns increases in arithmetic progression, as a function of the number of the syllables in the stem. High tone has become accentual in nature in Haya, in which only one high tone syllable per word is permitted in isolation. [...] and a bound accent language (Swahili).
new_statements.translation: (English original; the body of the paper is Japanese)
new_statements.citation: Kaji, Shigeki (梶茂樹) (2001). バンツー諸語の音調－そのタイプ－ / Tonal types of Bantu languages. 音声研究 (Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan) 5(1): 37-45. doi:10.24467/onseikenkyu.5.1_37
new_statements.reading: The one first-hand description of Tembo (Kaji, own fieldwork since 1976) classifies it as a polymoraic tone language: lexical H/L on every mora, patterns multiplying geometrically with length, explicitly opposed to accentual Haya and bound-accent Swahili. No word stress, culminative accent or fixed prominence position is posited for Tembo in any source read (Kaji 1978, 1994, 2001, 2021). If Tembo is added to the catalog, the coding supported is 'tone language, no word stress/fixed accent', with Kaji 2001 (or Kaji 2021 ch. 6) as the deciding source. Neither title-keyword item in the sweep says anything about Tembo: Philippson 1991 does not include Tembo in its sample and Möhlig 1969 concerns Shi/Dciriku/Hehe/Chaga; both are attached to temb1270 by Maho-code autotranslation of j.d.53 (Shi).

sources.quote: The Bantu languages of Africa show various tone types, ranging from pure tone languages to non-tonal languages. In this paper the author analyses the tone system of nouns in two languges: Tembo (J 57, eastern Congo) and Haya (J 22, northwestern Tanzania). With Tembo it is demonstrated that in this language each mora in principle should be marked either as high, low, falling or rising (the last two being combinations of high and low). The number of partterns increases in geometric progression. Tembo, therefore, can be characterized as a polymoraic tone language.
sources.note: First-hand (Kaji's own 1976-77 fieldwork): Tembo is a polymoraic tone language — every mora bears lexical H/L (or F/R), tone patterns multiply geometrically with word length — explicitly contrasted in the same summary with Haya (H 'has become accentual in nature', one H per word) and Swahili ('a bound accent language'). No word stress or culminative accent is posited for Tembo; no stress position is stated anywhere.

sources.quote: fn. 7: 例えば、標準スワヒリ語でも ńzi「蠅 sg.,pl.」のように、語頭の鼻音にもアクセントが来ることがある。しかし、これは単語が 2 音節という音声的理由からであって、単語が 3 音節以上だとアクセントが来ることはない [...] テンボ語で語頭の鼻音に H が来るのは、単語の長さとは関係ない音韻的理由からである。 — Introduction: b. TBU がモーラである言語 テンボ語、ウォライタ語（語尾） [Translation, fn. 7: In Standard Swahili too the accent can fall on a word-initial nasal, as in ńzi 'fly', but that is for the phonetic reason that the word is disyllabic; with three or more syllables the accent never falls there. That H falls on a word-initial nasal in Tembo is for a phonological reason unrelated to word length. — Introduction: languages whose TBU is the mora: Tembo, Wolaytta (suffixes).]
sources.locator: ch. 6 fn. 7 (p. ~113); Introduction sec. 5 (2a) and TBU list (b)
sources.note: Describes Tembo as a mora-counting tone language (H/L per mora, tone with lexical and grammatical function); the only mention of 'accent' contrasts Swahili's penultimate accent with Tembo's lexical H tone. No word stress is described for Tembo.

sources.citation: Kaji, Shigeki (梶茂樹) (1978). Tembo語の名詞のtone / Tone in Tembo nouns. アフリカ研究 (Journal of African Studies) 17: 34-57. doi:10.11619/africa1964.1978.34 [already on file; read here]
sources.quote: This paper, the data of which is based on fieldwork carried out by the auther in 1976-1977, treats tonal phenomena of nouns which, as far as the auther knows, characterize Tembo as a crucially distinct type of tone language among the Bantu languages hitherto studied [...] the tone of the prefixes shows up as high or low according to individual noun stems, because it is the stem which prescribes the tone of the prefix – the tone of the prefix being part of the stem.
sources.locator: p. 56-57, English summary; sec. 1.3 'Tembo語の場合'
sources.note: Treats Tembo (Mubuku/Mushunguti dialect, Misongi village) as an 'unrestricted'-type tone language (sec. 1.2-1.3: contrasts McCawley's 'true tone language' with 'pitch accent language' and places Tembo in the former; noun tone patterns grow as 3^n with syllable count). Nothing on stress; no accent position.
